new_groups.label: The embargo enforcing act and the non-intercourse laws, 1809
new_groups.definition: Two acts of the second session of the Tenth Congress, the act of 9 January 1809 to enforce the embargo and the act of 1 March 1809 to interdict commercial intercourse with Great Britain and France, the Treasury's circular of 3 March to the collectors on the second, and the act of 28 June 1809 of the first session of the Eleventh Congress that amended and continued it, as the 1809 papers printed them, most of them 'by authority'. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act of 9 January 1809 to enforce the embargo
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 9 January 1809 'to enforce and make more effectual an act, entitled, An act laying an embargo on all ships and vessels in the ports and harbors of the United States, and the several acts supplementary thereto': goods may not be put on board any vessel or carriage with intent to export them without a permit, and the collectors are given powers to seize, detain and require bonds.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act of 1 March 1809 to interdict commercial intercourse with Great Britain and France
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 1 March 1809 'to interdict the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France, and their dependencies; and for other purposes': the harbors and waters of the United States are closed to the public ships of both powers, and imports from them are prohibited, while the embargo is repealed except as to those powers; the President may renew trade with either if it revokes or modifies its edicts.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Treasury's circular of 3 March 1809 on the non-intercourse act
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Treasury Department's circular to the collectors of the customs, dated 3 March 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'I herewith transmit a printed copy of an act to interdict the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France', with directions section by section on how the collectors are to carry it out.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The act of 28 June 1809 continuing the non-intercourse act
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of 28 June 1809 'to amend and continue in force certain parts of the act, entitled "An act to interdict the commercial intercourse between the United States and Great Britain and France"': most of that act's sections continue in force to the end of the next session of Congress. Four papers had printed the Senate's bill a week earlier; its later sections differ from the act, so those printings are not included.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 17 January 1809 with letters of Canning and Pinkney
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's message to Congress of 17 January 1809: 'I communicate to Congress certain letters which passed between the British Secretary of State, Mr. Canning, and Mr. Pinkney, our minister plenipotentiary at London', with the two letters: Mr. Canning writes that he was 'desirous to ascertain whether in fact the Orders in Council of November had been known to the government of the United States previous to the message of the President proposing the Embargo', and Mr. Pinkney answers. Official documents; each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Report to the Massachusetts Senate on the act enforcing the embargo, 2 February 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from the Massachusetts Senate of 2 February 1809: its committee 'on the several Memorials from the people of a number of towns in this state, praying the interposition of the Legislature' reports resolves, the first that the act of 9 January to enforce the embargo 'is, in the opinion of the legislature, in many respects unjust, oppressive and unconstitutional, and not legally binding on the citizens of this state'. A state legislature's report and policy argument.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A Havana letter on the news from Spain, January 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Havana, 26 January 1809, first printed at Charleston: 'by the arrival yesterday of the ship Fortune from Liverpool ... the news from Spain is of a very disagreeable nature. Bonaparte is at the head of his armies, which appear to be victorious in all directions'. One writer's report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Madison's inaugural address, 4 March 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address James Madison delivered on taking the oath as President, 4 March 1809: 'Unwilling to depart from examples of the most revered authority, I avail myself of the occasion now presented, to express the profound impression made on me, by the call of my country'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: John Adams's letter of 13 March 1809: 'against any division of the Union'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter of the former President John Adams, Quincy, 13 March 1809, answering a letter of 3 March from two men of Northampton: 'Nothing remains to me but the right of private judgment ... I am, totis viribus [with my whole strength], against any division of the Union, by the North River, or by Delaware River, or by the Potomac, or any other river, or by any chain of mountains.' Some papers print the letter at length, others extracts. His own opinion.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: News from Cadiz by the ship Bordeaux: a battle near Valladolid

Two papers printed a shorter New York paragraph ('We learn by a gentleman who arrived here yesterday from Cadiz'). Reports at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 April 1809 on the arrangement
new_groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 19 April 1809, the government paper's own account: 'Since the arrival of Mr. Oakeley at Washington, Mr. Smith, Secretary of State, and Mr. Erskine, the British Minister, have been, we understand, every day engaged in discussions in relation to two points of difference between the United States and Great Britain', which had been settled; the notes that follow 'shew the happy result of these discussions'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The notes of Mr. Erskine and the Secretary of State, 17 to 19 April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the six notes exchanged at Washington between the British minister, D. M. Erskine, and the Secretary of State, Robert Smith, on 17, 18 and 19 April 1809, printed in one run (Nos. I to VI) and counted by the first: 'I have the honor to inform you, that I have received his Majesty's commands, to represent to the government of the United States, that his Majesty is animated by the most sincere desire for an adjustment of the differences'. Diplomatic notes, each in its writer's words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's proclamation of 19 April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Madison's proclamation of 19 April 1809: 'Whereas it is provided by the 11th section of the act of Congress entitled An act to interdict the commercial intercourse ...', it declares that the British orders in council 'will have been withdrawn' on 10 June 1809, after which trade with Great Britain may be renewed.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce's question and the Secretary of State's answer, April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of two letters printed together: Thomas Fitzsimons, president of the Chamber of Commerce at Philadelphia, to the Secretary of State, 22 April 1809 ('The proclamation ... has necessarily engaged the attention of the merchants of this city'), asking how it applies, and the Department of State's answer of 26 April. One paper prints the answer alone.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: France releases the American vessels held by its embargo, 1809
new_groups.definition: Two French documents of February 1809 printed by American papers in May: a French imperial decree of 25 February releasing American vessels detained in French ports by the embargo, and General Armstrong's letter from Paris of 23 February reporting it. Contains those two groups. The French government's decree and the American minister's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French decree of 25 February 1809 on American vessels
new_groups.definition: Printings of a French imperial decree of 25 February 1809: 'American vessels which have been detained in the ports of the Empire, solely by the (French) Embargo, are permitted to return directly to the U. States. This favor is not extended to such vessels as have been detained on account of irregular papers, or from any other cause.' The French government's decree.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Armstrong's letter of 23 February 1809: the French embargo raised
new_groups.definition: Printings of a copy of a letter of General Armstrong, the American minister at Paris, 23 February 1809: 'His Majesty has been pleased to raise the Embargo on American vessels within the ports of France and her dependencies and (the better to assure their direct return to the United States) to place them altogether at my disposition.' The American minister's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French thirty-third bulletin of the army of Spain: Tuy and Saragossa
new_groups.definition: Printings of the French army's thirty-third bulletin of the army of Spain, from the Paris Moniteur of 2 March 1809 (translated for the Boston Chronicle from a paper brought by the letter of marque L'Esperance): 'The Duke of Dalmatia arrived at Tuy on the 10th Feb. The whole province is quiet', then the siege of Saragossa: 'More than one third of the houses were in our possession'. The Alexandria Daily Gazette printed the Saragossa part alone as an extract, under the Boston Recorder's introduction. The French army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The War Department's circular to the governors on the militia, 29 April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the War Department's circular to the state governors, 29 April 1809: 'I am directed by the President of the United States to inform your Excellency that the detachment of ... Militia, made in pursuance of a communication to your Excellency from this Department' may be discharged. The papers print the copies sent to different governors (10,198 men for Virginia). The Portland Gazette calls it a circular 'for disbanding the Militia'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message to Congress, 23 May 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Madison's message at the opening of the first session of the Eleventh Congress, 23 May 1809: 'On this first occasion of meeting you, it affords me much satisfaction, to be able to communicate the commencement of a favorable change in our foreign relations'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: News from Canton: Admiral Drury's expedition to Macao
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of May 1809, by the ship Projector from Canton: 'an expedition fitted out at Bengal and Penang, under the direction of admiral Drury, for the purpose of taking possession of Macao', had arrived in September 1808, and the Portuguese governor refused to surrender the place. A report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British order in council of 26 April 1809 and the papers sent to the Senate
new_groups.definition: Britain's order in council of 26 April 1809, which revoked the orders of November 1807 and put the ports of France, Holland and Italy under blockade, the Board of Trade's explanation of it to the merchants trading to America, and the papers that President Madison sent to the Senate on 15 June: extracts of Mr. Pinkney's letters and Mr. Canning's, and Mr. Erskine's note on the order with the Secretary of State's answer. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British order in council of 26 April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the British order in council of 26 April 1809, from the London Gazette of 29 April: 'At the Court at the Queen's Palace, the 26th of April, 1809 ... Whereas his Majesty, by his order in council of the 11th November, 1807, was pleased ... to order' the restrictions of a blockade; the order revokes those orders and in their place puts the ports of France, Holland and Italy, and their colonies, under blockade. The British government's order.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Board of Trade's explanation of the order of 26 April
new_groups.definition: Printings of the explanation of the British order in council of 26 April 1809 given by the Board of Trade to a committee of merchants trading to America: 'By this regulation the United States may trade without interruption from British cruisers, with all the ports of Russia, Norway, and Sweden', the Baltic and other coasts. The papers printed it in different settings: as the Board's explanation ('Their Lordships state'), at the end of a London report of 28 April on the merchants' meeting with the lords of trade, or in a paragraph beginning 'It appears by the modification of the orders in council'. The British government's explanation, as reported from London.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message to the Senate of 15 June 1809, with letters of Mr. Pinkney and Mr. Canning
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Madison's message to the Senate of 15 June 1809, in compliance with its resolution of the 13th: 'I transmit extracts from letters from Mr. Pinkney to the Secretary of State, accompanied by letters and communications to him, from the British Secretary of State for the Foreign Department', with Mr. Canning's letter of 24 December 1808 ('I stated to you the probability that some alterations might be made in the orders in council'). One paper prints the documents without the message. Official documents; each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Mr. Erskine's note of 15 June 1809 on the order of 26 April, and the Secretary of State's answer
new_groups.definition: Printings of the British minister's note to the Secretary of State, Washington, 15 June 1809: 'I have the honor to inclose a copy of an order of his majesty in council issued on the 26th of April last ... I am enabled to assure you that it has no connexion whatever with the overtures which I have been authorised to make', with the Secretary of State's answer of the same day. Each note is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Austria goes to war, April 1809
new_groups.definition: Two Austrian state papers of April 1809 that American papers printed in June from London papers: the Emperor Francis's declaration on leaving Vienna, and the Archduke Charles's address to the German nation. Contains those two groups. Each is the Austrian government's own statement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Emperor Francis's declaration of war, Vienna, April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Emperor Francis's declaration on leaving Vienna, April 1809, headed 'DECLARATION OF WAR By Francis I. Emperor of Austria': 'Before his Imperial Majesty left this capital, he was pleased to issue the following proclamation ... People of Austria!—I leave my capital to join the brave defenders of the country'. The Austrian government's own statement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Archduke Charles's address to the German nation, April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of an address to the German nation that, as the papers print it, 'The Archduke Charles has issued': 'His Majesty the Emperor of Austria is forced to take up arms, because the French Emperor will not tolerate the existence of a State which does not acknowledge his supremacy of power'. The Austrian side's own statement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The first Austrian bulletin: the Archduke John in Friuli, April 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Austrian army's first bulletin, 'Dated Head Quarters Sacile, April 17', taken from London papers by way of Montreal and Boston: the Archduke John 'entered the territory of Frioule', and an action near Sacile 'terminated entirely to our advantage', with prisoners, cannon and eagles taken. The Austrian army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Britain disavows the April arrangement, July and August 1809
new_groups.definition: The papers of July and August 1809 on Britain's refusal to stand by the arrangement Mr. Erskine had made in April, as the papers printed them: a London report of 24 May that Mr. Canning told the Commons the agreement was not authorised, the order in council of 24 May, Mr. Canning's instructions to Mr. Erskine of 23 January as laid before Parliament, and the National Intelligencer's paragraph of 16 August on Mr. Erskine's letter of explanation. Contains those four groups. Each is one government's statement or its paper's account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, 24 May 1809: Canning tells the Commons the agreement was not authorised
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London newspaper report of 24 May 1809, headed 'AMERICAN AFFAIRS' and brought by way of Halifax: in the House of Commons 'lord Henry Petty put a question to Mr. Canning', who replied that the agreement made by Mr. Erskine 'was not made in conformity with the wishes of his majesty nor such as his majesty could approve of', and that American merchants who had acted on it would be protected. A newspaper's report of debate.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British order in council of 24 May 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the British order in council of 24 May 1809, from the London Gazette: the 'provisional agreement' made by the King's minister in America 'is not such as was authorised by his majesty's instructions, or such as his majesty can approve', but American vessels that sailed for Holland on the faith of it are not to be 'molested or interrupted'. The British government's order.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Canning's instructions to Erskine, 23 January 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of Mr. Canning's dispatch to Mr. Erskine, Foreign Office, 23 January 1809, as laid before Parliament and printed from London papers ('Copy of a dispatch from Mr. Secretary Canning to the hon. D. M. Erskine'): it names three conditions on which the orders in council could be withdrawn. The British government's instructions to its minister.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The National Intelligencer on Erskine's letter of explanation, August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 16 August 1809, the government paper's account: 'Mr. Secretary Smith received on the 14th inst. from Mr. Erskine a long and very satisfactory letter', in which Mr. Erskine explains why he did not lay his instructions before the American government; the paper adds its own view of Mr. Canning's dispatch.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A report from Martinique that the Toulon fleet was captured, July 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of 18 July 1809: the master of the sloop Henry, from Bermuda, 'informs us' that when he left Martinique on 27 June 'advices were received there of the capture of the Toulon fleet by lord Collingwood, consisting of 5 sail of the line, 6 or 7 frigates, and 30 transports'. A report at third hand; one paper said it did not believe it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The battle on the Danube, 21 and 22 May 1809: the French and the Austrian bulletins
new_groups.definition: The two armies' own accounts of the battle fought on 21 and 22 May 1809 near Vienna, on the left bank of the Danube, as American papers printed them in July and August from London papers: a London summary of the French tenth bulletin, and the Austrian official bulletin published by order of the Archduke Charles. Contains those two groups. Each is one side's account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French tenth bulletin (Ebersdorf, 23 May 1809), as summarised in London
new_groups.definition: Printings of an English newspaper's summary of the French army's tenth bulletin, 'Ebersdorf, May 23': 'After describing the form of the Danube at Ebersdorf, the bulletin states, that on the night of the 20th, the Emperor crossed the Danube'; the summary gives the French account of the two days' fighting and the English writer's comments. The French army's account, as summarised in London.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Austrian official bulletin of the battle, 23 May 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Austrian army's bulletin 'Published by order of his Imperial Highness, the Archduke Charles': 'the following preliminary report of the brilliant victory obtained the 21st and 22nd of May, is issued on the 23rd from the head quarters at Breitenlee'. Most papers head it 'AUSTRIAN OFFICIAL BULLETIN OF THE DEFEAT OF THE FRENCH'. The Austrian army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Buenos Ayres, 1809: reports of Liniers giving up the government
new_groups.definition: Two reports from Buenos Ayres printed by American papers in 1809, grouped by subject: a London paragraph of 12 June 'announcing the total defeat and submission of Liniers', and an extract of a letter from Rio de Janeiro of 3 August that a new Spanish viceroy had arrived and that Liniers 'gave up the government quietly'. Contains those two groups. Reports at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London, 12 June 1809: 'the total defeat and submission of Liniers'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London newspaper paragraph of 12 June 1809: 'Accounts have been received from Buenos Ayres, brought by a vessel from Cadiz, announcing the total defeat and submission of Liniers to the patriotic party, who had established a junta, proclaimed Ferdinand VII. and forced Liniers to sign a declaration that he would surrender the government'. A report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A letter from Rio de Janeiro, 3 August 1809: a new viceroy at Buenos Ayres
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Rio de Janeiro of 3 August 1809: a Spanish vessel from Buenos Ayres brings 'information that the new viceroy had arrived there from Spain', and that 'Liniers gave up the government quietly, and had retired on an annuity'. One writer's report at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's proclamation of 9 August 1809 and the Treasury circular
new_groups.definition: President Madison's proclamation of 9 August 1809, that the British orders in council had not been withdrawn as the British envoy had declared they would be, so that trade with Great Britain again fell under the acts that suspended it, and the Treasury's circular of the same day to the collectors, as the papers printed them, most of them together. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's proclamation of 9 August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Madison's proclamation of 9 August 1809: 'it is now officially made known to me that the said orders in council have not been withdrawn agreeably to the communication and declaration aforesaid', so that trade with Great Britain 'is to be considered as under the operation of the several acts by which such trade was suspended'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Treasury's circular to the collectors, 9 August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Treasury's circular to the collectors of the customs, 9 August 1809, signed by Albert Gallatin: 'You will herewith receive the copy of a Proclamation of the President'; the act of 28 June now applies to Great Britain as to France, 'any thing in my circular of 29th June last, to the contrary, notwithstanding', with rules for vessels that sailed on the faith of the April proclamation.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: An account from New Orleans of a planned revolt at the camp of Terre-aux-Boeufs, July 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of an unsigned account from New Orleans, dated 16 July 1809 (10 July in two papers), of 'a transaction' at the army's camp of Terre-aux-Boeufs: a lieutenant had reported 'that a general revolt was intended as soon as the men had received their pay', and the commanding general 'resolved as on a former occasion to anticipate the conspirators', had men drawn out on parade and ordered a court martial. In four papers it is a letter that opens by accusing two named men of 'exciting sedition among the troops'. One side's account; it names soldiers as accused.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The French twenty-fifth bulletin: the battle of Wagram, July 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the French army's twenty-fifth bulletin, 'Wolkersdorf, 8th July', translated from a Hamburg paper: the passage of the Danube from the island of Lobau on 4 July and the battles of 5 and 6 July. The French army's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lord Castlereagh's note to the Lord Mayor on the battle of Talavera, 14 August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the 'official note' sent to the Lord Mayor of London, Downing Street, 14 August 1809, as a New York paper of 30 September printed it from London papers brought by the ship Triton: the enemy 'attacked the combined armies posted at Talavera, on the 27th and 28th ult.' and 'on both days he was defeated with the most distinguished gallantry'. The British government's announcement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Spanish envoy Onis arrives and is not received, October 1809
new_groups.definition: Two New York reports of October 1809 on Don Luis de Onis, sent to the United States as minister by the Spanish Junta: the arrival of the Spanish frigate Cornelia that brought him, and the paragraph of 25 October that 'The new Spanish Minister, Don Onis, has not been received by our government.' Contains those two groups. Reports.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, 4 October 1809: the Spanish frigate Cornelia brings Don Onis
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York report of 4 October 1809: 'Late last night the Spanish frigate Cornelia … arrived at the quarantine ground. She sailed from Cadiz on the 20th of August. This vessel has brought out his excellency Don Lewis de Onis, minister plenipotentiary and envoy extraordinary from his Catholic majesty Ferdinand the 7th'. A report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, 25 October 1809: Don Onis 'has not been received by our government'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of late October 1809: 'At a late hour last night, the following fact came to our knowledge. The new Spanish Minister, Don Onis, has not been received by our government'; it says the President would not receive him while Spain remained 'in its present unsettled state'. A newspaper's report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British expedition to the Scheldt: Lord Chatham's two dispatches, 1809
new_groups.definition: Two dispatches of the Earl of Chatham, commanding the British expedition to the Scheldt, as the London Gazette published them and American papers printed them in October 1809: the dispatch of 15 August from Middleburg on the surrender of Flushing, and the dispatch of 29 August from Batz on closing his operations. Contains those two groups. The British commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lord Chatham's dispatch of 15 August 1809: the surrender of Flushing
new_groups.definition: Printings of the London Gazette's notice, Downing Street, 19 August 1809, of a dispatch from Lieutenant General the Earl of Chatham, dated headquarters, Middleburg, 15 or 16 August: 'the batteries before Flushing being completed', a fire was opened on the 13th, and the town surrendered. The British commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Lord Chatham's dispatch of 29 August 1809: the operations closed
new_groups.definition: Printings of the London Gazette's notice of 2 September 1809 of a dispatch from the Earl of Chatham, dated headquarters, Batz, 29 August: the enemy's force near Antwerp is too strong, and 'however mortifying to me to see the progress arrested of an army, from whose good conduct and valor I had every thing to hope, I feel that my duty left me no other course than to close my operations here'. The British commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A Russian decree on the papers of neutral vessels, June 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Russian decree of 14 June 1809, sent by the American consul at St. Petersburg to a New York commercial house 'with a request that it may be published': every captain entering a Russian port must prove ship and cargo neutral by his papers, because 'the enemy has found means to misuse neutral bottoms for the benefit of his trade'. The Russian government's decree.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Nashville Clarion on the death of Governor Meriwether Lewis, October 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the Nashville Clarion's account of 20 October 1809: 'To record the untimely end of a brave and prudent officer, a learned scholar and scientific gentleman this column of the Clarion is ushered to the world in black. On the night of the 10th instant Meriwether Lewis, esq. Governor-general of Upper Louisiana, on his way to Washington city', died at a house on the road; the paper says 'he had shot himself', and adds a sketch of his career. A newspaper's account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The British minister Jackson and the end of the correspondence, November 1809
new_groups.definition: Three items of November 1809 on the end of the correspondence between the Secretary of State and the British minister, Francis James Jackson: the National Intelligencer's statement of 13 November, its article of 15 November that 'All negotiation with the British government at this place is suspended', and Jackson's circular of 13 November to the British consuls. Contains those three groups. The Intelligencer's paragraphs are the government paper's account; the circular is the British minister's own.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The National Intelligencer's statement of 13 November 1809 on the correspondence with Jackson
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 13 November 1809, the government paper's account: 'In the course of the correspondence, which, it seems, has taken place between the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson', the British minister repeated what the paper calls a 'gross insinuation', and the Secretary informed him 'that no further communications would be received from him'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The National Intelligencer, 15 November 1809: 'All negotiation … is suspended'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the National Intelligencer's leading article of 15 November 1809: 'All negotiation with the British government at this place is suspended by one of those events which we should call extraordinary'; it says the minister offered 'the grossest insult' to the nation, and quotes Vattel on what a sovereign may do when a foreign minister offends him. The government paper's argument.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Jackson's circular to the British consuls, 13 November 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter headed 'CIRCULAR', Washington, 13 November 1809, from the British minister F. J. Jackson to the British consuls: 'I have to inform you with much regret, that the facts which it has been my duty to state in my official correspondence with Mr. Smith, have been deemed by the President of the United States to afford a sufficient motive for breaking off an important negotiation'; he says he gave no offence and will withdraw to New York. The British minister's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Champagny's letter to Armstrong, Altenburg, 22 August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter of the French minister of foreign affairs, Champagny, to General Armstrong, Altenburg, 22 August 1809, in a translation from European papers: 'His Majesty, understanding that you are about to despatch a ship to the United States, commands me to make known to you the unalterable principles which have and will regulate his conduct in the great question respecting neutrals'. The French government's statement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message of 29 November 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Madison's message to Congress at the opening of its session, 29 November 1809: 'At the period of our last meeting, I had the satisfaction of communicating an adjustment with one of the principal belligerent nations'; it reports that the British government did not carry the arrangement out and that communications with its new minister ended, and speaks of France, the treasury and the militia.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The documents sent to Congress with the message of 29 November 1809
new_groups.definition: The diplomatic papers that President Madison sent to Congress with his message of 29 November 1809, as the papers printed them over one to four issues, in the publication's order: Mr. Erskine's letters of July and August with the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Treasury; the correspondence of the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson from 9 October to 13 November; the Secretary of State's letter to Mr. Pinkney of 23 November; and General Armstrong's letters from Paris with Champagny's. Contains those four groups, each counted by its first document. Each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The documents, part one: Mr. Erskine's letters of July and August 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the first part of the documents sent to Congress with the President's message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document, Mr. Erskine's letter to the Secretary of State of 31 July 1809 ('I have the honor to inclose to you a copy of an order, which was passed by His Majesty in Council'); the letters of July and August between Mr. Erskine, the Secretary of State and the Secretary of the Treasury follow it. Each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The documents, part two: the Secretary of State and Mr. Jackson, October and November 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the second part of the documents sent with the message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document: 'THE SECRETARY OF STATE TO MR. JACKSON … Department of State, October 9th, 1809. Sir—An arrangement, as to the revocation of the British Orders in Council, as well as to the satisfaction required in the case of the attack on the Chesapeake frigate, has been made in due form'. Eight letters follow to the Secretary's of 8 November, which ends the correspondence, with two notes delivered for Mr. Jackson by his secretary. Each letter is its writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1809 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The documents, part three: the Secretary of State to Mr. Pinkney, 23 November 1809
new_groups.definition: Printings of the third part of the documents sent with the message of 29 November 1809, counted by its first document: the Secretary of State's letter to Mr. Pinkney in London, 23 November 1809, giving the government's account of the correspondence with Mr. Jackson and asking that he be recalled. dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1809 that reach 4 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 241 items in 7 or more papers by the finder's count). Because the acts of the second session of the Tenth Congress and other documents sit in families that began in 1808, the same script was also run with year 1808 over the 1809 pages (items_from_1808.json: 54 items in 7 or more papers). Two AI reviewers read the items of each half of the year and proposed the stories, checking each count item by item with phrase searches over all 4,172 pages of 1809 in both transcriptions; their proposals were merged and checked again here (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json), and every hit not accepted was read. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1807 and 1808: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs. Items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months and the main kinds of news. Stories are counted item by item; where one publication holds several documents, or several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story, or, where the papers always printed them in one run, the publication's own parts are the groups, each counted by its first document (as 1808 did). A sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7. The Kentucky Gazette and General Advertiser (to 4 April) and the Kentucky Gazette (from 11 April) are one paper under two catalogue numbers and are counted once. Every story alike: no item was left out for its subject.

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of 1809 through their enacting formula and through titles recited in other acts, proclamations and debates (items of 9 to 12 papers and up to 101 printings). Counted by its own first section, no act reaches 9: the act to enforce the embargo and the non-intercourse act are in 8 papers, the act of 28 June in 7; the appropriation, relief, land and military acts in 5 or 6. The Senate's bill of June 1809, printed in four papers a week before the act, is not counted: its later sections differ from the act.
counted_item_by_item.The December documents: The documents sent to Congress with the message of 29 November hold about twenty letters, which every paper printed in the publication's order over one to four issues. They were grouped by the publication's four parts, each counted by its first document; each letter's own count is in the second reader's proposal (12 letters in 9 or 10 papers).
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: Several finder items of 9 or more papers join different texts that share words: Canning's instructions and the Secretary of State's letter that quotes their conditions; the Intelligencer's statement of 13 November, the Secretary's letter of 8 November and later commentary; Jackson's circular and his secretary's note of the same day; the proclamations of April and August and the act they recite. Each text was counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote an item: Editorials, speeches, debate reports and later documents that quote or recite an item were not counted: for example the essay that quotes Erskine's note of 17 April in the National Intelligencer of 26 July and the Delaware Gazette of 29 July, the commentary of 28 November in the New Hampshire Gazette that repeats the Intelligencer's words of 16 August, and Macon's bill of December, which recites the title of the act of 28 June.
counted_item_by_item.Printed again: A paper that printed an item again counts each printing: the Virginia Argus reprinted Erskine's April notes on 18 August, the National Intelligencer printed the message of 29 November twice in one issue (pages 1 and 5), the Alexandria Daily Gazette printed it on 29 and 30 November, and the proclamation and circular of 9 August were printed again in December.
